top.line: The human-sounding voice comes from four inputs, not tricks
top.para: Asked how the AI sounds so human, I answer that the voice is four inputs: a corpus of 86 articles and about 347,000 words, voice memos carrying how I think, seven wording rules in the behaviour policy, and me reading everything. Claude then explains, in its own voice, why it works and why it cannot transfer.

short.line: Corpus, memos, seven rules and a reader make it
short.para: The corpus supplies vocabulary and shape: 86 articles, 51 from voice memos. The memo supplies the thinking. Seven rules, each once a correction, are restored after every summary. I read everything, so wrong words become rules. Recent corrections are about content, not language, and the method transfers while the voice does not.

inputs.line: Memos carry the thinking; rules and reading keep it
inputs.para: The model writes on top of 86 linked articles and years of earlier writing, so terms are defined, not guessed. Memos keep my phrases, tangents and order of thought. Seven rules, such as British English and no absolutes, sit in the policy file and validator. I read every article twice, and the loop runs daily.

corrections.line: Corrections shifted from wording to content, as rules accumulated
corrections.para: Since the session's last summary there were 98 messages from me, 25 over 300 words and five Otter transcripts of about 4,900 words. In the last two days only one correction was about a word, "prose"; the rest were about content, direction and facts. A rules file fixes language once, while content corrections are new thinking.

claude.line: Claude says memos work because they show the path
claude.para: Writing in its own voice, Claude says this is not imitation: it has the linked articles, the memo, specific word rules and a known reader. A memo shows how Dinis got there, so the tangents are his connections. Nothing is trained; the voice is one session's context and cannot be handed to another author.

limits.line: One session's counts, judged only by its author
limits.para: The counts are from one session after its last summary, with corrections classified by reading them. The model's account of itself is not a measurement. Only I have judged whether the articles sound like me. Nothing is trained: the voice is context that ends with the session, hence the rules file.

sources.line: Sources: a voice memo and the session transcript counts
sources.para: The piece comes from a voice memo of 12 October 2026, after showing the walkthrough to the person it was written for. Counts are from the site's article sources and the session transcript that day; wording rules from the behaviour policy. Related pieces include Re-anchoring and How much of this did I write?
